title: Women Take Power in Mexico. Seriously. Rosa Icela, Ariadna, Ernestina, Laura Itzel…
author: Sugeyry Romina Gándara
content:
_This article by[Sugeyry Romina
Gándara](https://www.sinembargo.mx/author/sugeyry_gandara/) originally
appeared in the [September 6, 2026 edition of
SinEmbargo](https://www.sinembargo.mx/4864774/las-mujeres-toman-el-poder-en-
serio-rosa-icela-ariadna-ernestina-laura-itzel/), one of Mexico's leading
independent digital news outlets._

In her second year in government, Claudia Sheinbaum has various figures within
her administration who show that the appointment of women to decision-making
spaces is not limited to a matter of numbers or to complying with the rules of
gender parity.

Ernestina Godoy, for example, heads the Attorney General's Office of the
Republic; Rosa Icela Rodríguez, the Interior Ministry; Ariadna Montiel, who
was at the Welfare Ministry, is now the head of Morena; Laura Itzel Castillo,
who has just left the Presidency of the Senate, will be Secretary for Women;
and Alicia Bárcena Ibarra heads the Ministry of the Environment.

Among these figures, perhaps the one who best exemplifies this situation is
Rosa Icela Rodríguez, the current Interior Minister. Although she had already
held a high-level post during the administration of Andrés Manuel López
Obrador, when she was in charge of the Ministry of Security and Citizen
Protection (SSPC), today she heads the Interior Ministry, one of the most
influential positions within the federal cabinet.

It is not the first time a woman has held this ministry. During López
Obrador's government, Olga Sánchez Cordero was the first to lead it. At that
time, the department went through a process of fragmentation, in which the
political weight it had traditionally concentrated was transferred to other
areas of government, particularly to the Legal Counsel's Office, then headed
by Julio Scherer Ibarra, while the ministry took charge of issues related to
human rights and religious affairs.

The situation became even more evident when Sánchez Cordero left the Interior
Ministry and López Obrador placed Adán Augusto López in charge, one of his
trusted men and also a member of his political group from Tabasco. With him,
the department recovered part of its role as the body in charge of domestic
policy.

Nevertheless, now that space, with all its functions, is once again headed by
a woman: Rosa Icela Rodríguez, an official close to President Claudia
Sheinbaum and with experience in areas that for years were associated with
male figures.

For Andrea Samaniego, a Doctor in Political and Social Sciences from UNAM and
currently a professor at the FCPyS, this point is relevant because the change
does not consist solely of there being women holding public office, but in the
fact that more and more women are reaching ministries considered strategic.

**“One of the central points had always been for us women to arrive. Once we
have the first female President of Mexico, what do we observe? That there are
indeed more and more women in these cabinet posts, as heads of the Federal
Public Administration,”** she explained.

Samaniego pointed out, moreover, that these figures have not arrived at simple
posts, but at spaces that have traditionally been attributed to men and that,
by that same tradition, are considered male domains. **“The hypothesis starts
from the idea that it is not only about putting women in posts, but that they
are really placed in positions of power,”** she explained.

> It is not only about putting women in posts, but that they are really placed
> in positions of power.
>
> Andrea Samaniego

For the specialist, the situation carries greater weight when the current
administration is viewed as a whole, since, in terms of parity, one can even
speak of a situation different from the one usually posed: there are more
women than men in some spaces of the federal government.

**“In this administration we see many women. On the matter of parity it is
even not met, but because there are more women. We have an administration that
is not gender-balanced because there are more women, and that is striking,”**
she noted.

Samaniego recalled that during the previous administration the cabinet began
as gender-balanced, but the changes made as the six-year term advanced altered
that composition and it later ceased to be so. Something similar frequently
occurs in state and municipal governments, where the parity criterion in the
leadership of administrations is also not always maintained, the UNAM
professor elaborated.

## Rosa Icela, the Operator

Rosa Icela Rodríguez is one of the most visible figures of the current
administration. Today she heads the Interior Ministry after having been in
charge of Security.

**“Rosa Icela comes from a ministry that is also assumed to answer to, or to
belong to, a male space, such as Security, and now she is at the Interior
Ministry,”** posited the specialist Andrea Samaniego.

Rosa Icela Rodríguez Velázquez, originally from Xilitla, San Luis Potosí, was
born in 1959. She was a journalist and public servant. She studied at the
Carlos Septién García School of Journalism and worked at media outlets such as
La Afición, El Universal and La Jornada.

In public service she has worked mainly in two areas: public security and
citizen services. Two fields that, although they may seem distant, form part
of the career with which she came to hold high-level posts.

During López Obrador's government she headed the Ministry of Security and
Citizen Protection, from which she became the first woman to hold that
position. However, that Security Ministry did not have the same powers it
currently has.

During the previous administration, several of the operational security tasks,
as well as the role of the National Guard, were linked to the Ministry of
National Defense, in a process of greater military participation in public
security duties. With the arrival of Omar García Harfuch at the Ministry of
Security and Citizen Protection, the department received greater powers
following a reform.

With Claudia Sheinbaum she reached the Interior Ministry, a position that
represents another step within that career in decision-making spaces.
Rodríguez's profile in that post has even placed her on the radar of those who
consider that she could become a natural pre-candidate for the governorship of
San Luis Potosí, her home state.

The case of Rosa Icela Rodríguez thus adds to a broader picture of Sheinbaum's
administration: the presence of women in power no longer only as a matter of
representation, but at the head of some of the most influential areas within
the federal government.

## Ernestina Godoy, the Attorney General

Another of the notable figures is that of the Attorney General of the
Republic, Ernestina Godoy, who took office after the then Attorney General
Alejandro Gertz Manero **“was invited to leave the post”** to take up an
embassy in the United Kingdom. The vacancy fell to Godoy, who had already been
Attorney General of Mexico City.

The move completed an operation that specialists considered strategic to bring
to the federal government a formula that had already paid off for Sheinbaum
when she was Head of Government: the Sheinbaum-Harfuch-Godoy team. That team
was credited with results in the administration of justice and security in
Mexico City.

Andrea Samaniego explained that Godoy is a figure close to the President and
considered that this coordination is relevant in the administration of
justice, particularly in the face of high-impact crimes.

**“As the President herself has indicated, there is no subordination, but
there must indeed be coordination,”** she noted.

The specialist also stressed that Godoy's case breaks with the idea that
justice areas are spaces that belong to men. She explained that for years it
has been considered that women could be more sentimental or take a more
flexible stance, but that Godoy's career shows that the performance of these
functions does not depend on gender, but on the capacity to carry them out.

**“Jobs do not have this question of gender; rather, it is a question of
capacity and of who can perform the functions they require,”** she maintained.

> Jobs do not have this question of gender; rather, it is a question of
> capacity and of who can perform the functions they require.
>
> Andrea Samaniego

Ernestina Godoy, a lawyer of Guerrero origin, has built her career on the
left. During her career she advised victims of the 1985 earthquake and took
part in the San Andrés Accords following the Zapatista uprising in Chiapas,
where she met figures who today form part of the so-called Fourth
Transformation, among them Andrés Manuel López Obrador and Claudia Sheinbaum.

When she was Attorney General in Sheinbaum's administration she led
investigations related to the so-called Real Estate Cartel, centered in the
Benito Juárez borough, a borough she knew well, since she was Director of
Legal Affairs and Verification between 2018 and 2021.

The investigations into the Real Estate Cartel were one of the main works of
her tenure, and generated a political and legislative dispute that prevented
her re-election as Attorney General of Mexico City for a term running until
2028.

Now, Godoy heads the Attorney General's Office of the Republic, one of the key
institutions of the federal government, and is part of the female figures who
hold positions of power in Claudia Sheinbaum's administration.

## Ariadna Montiel

Ariadna Montiel, who since 2018 had held various posts until ending up in
charge of the Welfare Ministry, one of the pillar departments of the social
programs that have given the Fourth Transformation its popularity, was this
year sent to bring order to Morena ahead of the 2027 elections.

In May of this year she was named head of the party, following the wear and
tear that its leaders, Luisa María Alcalde and Andrés Manuel López Beltrán,
had suffered.

President Claudia Sheinbaum herself made the strategic move by offering Luisa
María Alcalde the Legal Counsel's Office, in order to send Montiel to Morena,
while Citlalli Hernández, who had been Secretary for Women under Claudia
Sheinbaum, also returned to the party leadership as Secretary of Organization.

The change placed Montiel at the head of Morena after having held for years
one of the central departments of the Fourth Transformation's social programs.

For Andrea Samaniego, her experience heading the Welfare Ministry is also
relevant because of the handling of resources. She noted that Montiel was in
charge of the budget of the social programs and that this knowledge can give
the party another electoral reading.

**“She seems to me a figure who indeed knows about resources, about money,
since she managed the largest budget, the budget of the Welfare programs, and
from there she moves to the Morena party,”** she noted.

The specialist explained that this knowledge could allow her to identify in
which municipalities the resources of the social programs are concentrated
and, based on that, to steer or reinforce Morena's electoral strategy.

Samaniego also stressed that Welfare, although it is not the Finance Ministry,
is a department that handles many resources, so the fact that Montiel was in
charge also goes against the idea that these kinds of posts do not belong to
women.

**“Rather, she demonstrates that indeed, we come back to it, it is a question
of capacity,”** she noted.

Montiel is an architect and developed her political career in the capital's
PRD structures. She was Secretary of Youth, Secretary of Finance and Secretary
of Political Relations and Alliances of that party. She was also alternate
Senator to María Rojo, director general of the capital's Passenger Transport
Network, Deputy in the Legislative Assembly of the Federal District and
federal Deputy.

In 2018, the then President-elect Andrés Manuel López Obrador announced that
Montiel would be Undersecretary of the Welfare Ministry. In 2022 she took over
as head of the department and was later ratified by Claudia Sheinbaum, until
May 2026, when she left to lead the maroon party.

## Laura Itzel Castillo

Laura Itzel Castillo, who was serving as President of the Senate, joins
Mexico's Cabinet as Secretary for Women.

She is a figure who has carried political interest from the cradle: she is the
daughter of a mythical figure of the Mexican left, Heberto Castillo, and of
Teresa Juárez, representative of Andrés Manuel López Obrador when he went
before the Chamber of Deputies over the desafuero (removal of immunity)
process.

An architect by training, Laura Itzel Castillo has built a broad career in
public service and elected office. Between 1991 and 1994 she was part of the
Assembly of Representatives of what was then the Federal District and later
served as federal Deputy in the LVII and LXI legislatures.

She was also Borough Chief of Coyoacán between 1999 and 2000, before joining
the capital's government. Later she headed the Ministry of Urban Development
and Housing of what was then the Federal District, where she was in charge of
issues related to the capital's territorial planning.

In recent years she directed Mobility System 1 (M1) of Mexico City,
responsible for an important part of public transport. She currently serves as
President of the Senate of the Republic.

For Andrea Samaniego, although Laura Itzel is not a figure in the great
spotlight, she does have broad experience and knowledge in different fields.

**“That does not mean she is not a figure with a track record. She has a broad
career; she has a lot of mileage in politics,”** she noted.

## Other Figures

Samaniego also highlighted other figures who hold key posts within the federal
government, among them Raquel Buenrostro Sánchez, who was named Secretary of
Anti-Corruption and Good Governance.

Buenrostro, an economist and mathematician, was head of the SAT (the tax
authority) during the government of Andrés Manuel López Obrador, a period in
which the litigation against Ricardo Salinas Pliego to make him pay taxes
began. **“Like all the figures I have mentioned to you, she has a lot of
experience in every field. She is known for being a firm hand,”** Samaniego
noted.

The specialist considered that Buenrostro's case also breaks with the idea
that women can be more lax or soft when exercising positions of
responsibility.

**“Because sometimes it is thought that we women are going to be more lax or
softer with people, and that we will be swayed by our hearts, and she, in the
posts she has held, has been tough,”** she explained.

> Sometimes it is thought that we women are going to be more lax or softer
> with people… she, in the posts she has held, has been tough.
>
> Andrea Samaniego

Another of the figures she highlighted was Alicia Bárcena, at the head of the
Ministry of Environment and Natural Resources (Semarnat), a department that,
she said, faces complex challenges because of the work with different groups
and because of the conflicts that can arise around environmental policies.

Samaniego noted that Bárcena has had a difficult job, particularly in the face
of tourism or industrial projects that can raise questions over their
environmental impact and over future rights. She also mentioned Rosaura Ruiz,
at the head of the Ministry of Science, Humanities, Technology and Innovation,
of whom she stressed that she is a woman devoted to science.
